summary: Defines an XML document format that reports a change in an XCAP-managed document, giving the document's former and new entity tags. It can include differences using an XML patch format. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A note says which document changed, how it looked before and after, and even what exactly was edited.

questions: how to report xcap document changes
what is an xcap diff document
what is the xcap-diff media type
subtitle: An XML format that tells a client which XCAP document changed, its old and new ETags, and optionally exactly what changed.

tldr.problem: When several clients edit the same XCAP document, such as a presence list, every client's cached copy can go stale, and a plain content-indirection notice cannot say whether a change was the client's own or how the document changed.
tldr.mechanism: An XCAP diff document is an XML document with an xcap-diff root that lists document elements carrying the document's previous and new entity tags, optionally with XML patch operations, plus element and attribute entries that show existing content.
tldr.outcome: A client can keep a local copy in step with the server using fewer transmissions and less bandwidth. The format says nothing about transport; a SIP event package (RFC 5875) is the usual carrier. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 5874 is a Proposed Standard from May 2010. The metadata for this RFC lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. Its usual transport, a SIP event package, is described in RFC 5875.

sections.title: Why a Change Format Is Needed
sections.content:
The XML Configuration Access Protocol (XCAP, RFC 4825) lets clients manipulate XML documents stored on a server. These documents serve as configuration for application protocols. The RFC's main example is a resource list (a presence list) that a Resource List Server uses, which clients edit to add and remove friends.

The trouble starts when several clients edit one document. A client usually keeps a copy in memory to show the user, and that copy becomes stale when another client changes the document. Every client holding a copy needs to learn about the change so it can fetch the latest version.

One possible answer is a content indirection object (RFC 4483). The RFC rejects it for two reasons. It identifies the new version with a MIME Content-ID, which is not the entity tag that XCAP uses for versioning, so a client cannot easily tell its own edit from someone else's. And it only says that a document changed, not how.

The XCAP diff document fixes both problems. It reports which document changed with its former and new entity tags, and it can carry the differences as XML patch operations (RFC 5261) that turn the cached version into the new one. The intent is to cut bandwidth and the number of separate transmissions.
sections.plainLanguage: When your friends change a shared notebook, your own copy goes out of date. This note tells you what changed so you do not have to copy the whole notebook again.

sections.title: Who Does What
sections.content:
The RFC defines a small cast of roles. The XCAP server manages documents and their entity tags and usually contains an integrated diff notifier, the part that generates diff documents and sends them to a client within a session. The diff client consumes the diff documents to build a locally cached document equal to a specific version stored at the server. It is typically a SIP user agent and an XCAP client.

An ETag here is a strong HTTP entity tag whose value the XCAP server sets. The server assigns a new ETag to every document version, so the ETag acts as a version identifier. A locally cached resource is a copy, typically downloaded by HTTP, that may have been patched locally from diff information.

Logical equality of documents is judged by their canonical form with comments, the same way XCAP does it, when the format is used to patch cached copies.
sections.plainLanguage: There is the keeper of the notebook, a messenger who spots changes, and a friend with a photocopy. Each page has a version stamp so everyone can tell which version they hold.

sections.title: Structure of an XCAP Diff Document
sections.content:
A diff document is XML 1.0 that MUST be well-formed, SHOULD be valid and MUST be encoded in UTF-8. Its namespace is the URN urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:xcap-diff. The root element is <xcap-diff> with one mandatory attribute, xcap-root, the XCAP root URI of the documents that changed. One diff document can only describe changes within one XCAP root. Unknown extension content MUST be ignored by the diff client.

Inside the root come any number of <document>, <element> and <attribute> elements. A <document> has a mandatory sel attribute (a relative path from the XCAP root) and optional new-etag and previous-etag attributes. Its content is either a sequence of <add>, <replace> and <remove> patch operations defined in RFC 5261, or a <body-not-changed> element meaning the document got a new ETag but its content did not change.

If several <document> elements name the same document, their patches MUST be applicable in the order given, so a client never has to sort patch instructions.

The combination of attributes tells the client what happened. Both ETags with patches means the document was patched and the patch is included. A new ETag alone means the document was created or exists. A previous ETag alone means it was removed, and then new-etag MUST NOT be present. The two ETags need not be consecutive at the server: a diff can summarise a series of operations as long as running them in order turns the old version into the new one.

<element> and <attribute> entries show the existing content of an XML element or attribute. Each has a mandatory sel and an optional exists flag. When exists is absent the component still exists. An <element> holds the located element as its child. In the corner case where the content cannot be shown, for example because it is too large, the <element> MUST have no child nodes.
sections.plainLanguage: Each note names a page and gives its old and new version stamps. If there is only a new stamp, the page is new. If there is only an old stamp, the page was thrown away.

sections.title: Rules for Exchanging Diff Documents
sections.content:
A diff client MUST apply a state change only when the entity tags match octet-by-octet according to the table of cases. If it notices errors or inconsistencies while applying changes, it SHOULD tear down the session.

Delivery has to be reliable. The client MUST be able to apply all changes in the same chronological order that occurred at the server. With an unreliable transport that retransmits, duplicates MUST be dropped, and if a diff delivery is lost the session MUST be torn down.

A notifier does not have to report every intermediate version. It MAY skip a version of a rapidly changing document, provided it reports consistently. For example, if a document went through versions a, b and c and the notifier skips b, the next notification carries the ETag of a as previous-etag and that of c as new-etag, with optional content changes from a to c.

The format does not say which resources a notifier should report or whether content changes are reported. Typically a client starts a session with a resource listing request, compares it with its cache, and downloads documents that are missing or have different ETags. Several round trips may be needed before full synchronization, especially for rapidly changing resources.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages must arrive in order and none may be lost. The messenger may skip a middle version, as long as the old and new stamps still line up with what you hold.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The appendix walks through a server with documents for two users. A listing is a diff document with only new-etag values. After Joe adds a document, a diff with just a new-etag signals creation. After he edits it, a diff with previous-etag and new-etag signals a modification without showing the change. After he deletes it, a diff with only previous-etag signals removal.

To show actual changes, the appendix has Joe make three separate element insertions, each producing a new ETag. The diff can report them aggregated as one <add> from the first ETag to the last, which loses the intermediate history. Alternatively it can report three chained <document> elements, one per ETag change, which preserves the full history in chronological order.

Finally, <attribute> and <element> entries show component contents. When Joe deletes an attribute, the diff reports it with exists='0'.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show a friend adding, changing and deleting pages, and how each action becomes a short note with the right version stamps.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A diff can contain the changes of a document, so if the document is sensitive and needs confidentiality, integrity or authentication, so does the diff. The transporting protocol must provide enough security. Confidential XCAP documents are typically moved over TLS, and RFC 4825 has further detail. Diff notifiers MUST obey XCAP authorization rules, in practice the read privilege rules, and transport SHOULD be encrypted.

When content changes are reported, all security considerations of RFC 5261 apply. Very frequent updates or many diff clients per subscribed resource create a denial-of-service possibility, which efficient patch processing and throttling can reduce. When SIP event packages carry the format, end-to-end SIP encryption such as S/MIME SHOULD be used, and otherwise TLS between elements is RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: The note can reveal private things from the notebook, so it must only go to people allowed to read the page, and it should travel in a sealed envelope.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The RFC registers three things. The media type is application/xcap-diff+xml, with a file extension of .xdf, and it inherits its parameters and encoding rules from application/xml as defined in RFC 3023. The XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:xcap-diff is registered as a URN sub-namespace, and the schema is registered as urn:ietf:params:xml:schema:xcap-diff. The schema XML is the sole content of Section 4.
sections.plainLanguage: The format gets its own official name tag, so computers everywhere know what these notes are.

data.code:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<xcap-diff xmlns="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:xcap-diff"
           xcap-root="http://xcap.example.com/">

 <document previous-etag="terteer" new-etag="huwiias"
           sel="tests/users/sip:joe@example.com/another_document"/>

</xcap-diff>
